handoff.purpose: Continue _remove_tree_no_follow's directory drain with re-verification, define remove_tree_no_follow, GitWorktreeManager.__init__, _run_git, allocation bookkeeping, and containment refusals.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager
symbols.note: Manages isolated Git worktrees; constructor caches repo identity and ancestor identities.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager.__init__
symbols.note: Resolves repo_path, initializes in-memory allocations, records repo and ancestor identities.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._run_git
symbols.note: Runs a git command via subprocess, returns stdout, raises RuntimeError on failure.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._alloc_file
symbols.note: Returns hashed JSON filename for a worktree path.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._record_allocation
symbols.note: Writes allocation record BEFORE git worktree add.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._write_allocation
symbols.note: Creates alloc dir and writes JSON record.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._read_allocation
symbols.note: Reads and validates allocation record; returns None if missing or invalid.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._refuse
symbols.note: Constructs and returns WorktreeContainmentError with a standard message.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._reach_chain
symbols.note: Returns path chain from worktree_root to target; raises refusal if not within.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._refuse_if_repo_adjacent
symbols.note: Raises refusal if candidate is within or contains repo_path.

claims.text: Children before parents: a parent is always popped before its children are queued, so its index is lower.
claims.why: The code iterates directories in reversed order after appending children during the walk; the comment describes the queue order, which is consistent with the pop-based BFS.

claims.text: Every entry here was classified when it was POPPED, which for the first one drained is the ENTIRE walk ago
claims.why: The walk appends entries as they are encountered; by the time the first directory is drained, its classification occurred during the initial walk, which is 'an entire walk ago'.

claims.text: os.rmdir resolves its path argument through a reparse point in an intermediate component exactly as os.scandir does.
claims.why: This is a platform behaviour claim about os.rmdir and os.scandir; this chunk does not contain the implementation of either, so it cannot be verified here.

claims.text: An unverified drain therefore lets a junction renamed over an already-drained subdirectory redirect every remaining rmdir out of the tree. Measured, 3/3, end to end through cleanup_worktree: 3000 empty directories removed inside a stand-in primary checkout, reported as success.
claims.why: The attack scenario and the measured result refer to behaviour outside this chunk (the walk, the stand-in checkout, and cleanup_worktree). The comment asserts a vulnerability that this code mitigates via _verify_reachable, but the claim's evidence is not in this chunk.

claims.text: If _is_reparse_point(directory) is true, 'this directory was emptied by the walk above, so whatever is here now is not what was emptied, and the link is not the manager's to delete. Refuse, and report the tree as partially removed.'
claims.why: The code raises WorktreeRemovalRace with a message that matches the comment, and no repair is attempted.

claims.text: The one caller outside this module today is the default pytest gate's scratch directory (:mod:`daedalus.spine.attempt`), which is created in %TEMP% under a predictable daedalus-gate- prefix while candidate code is running as this same user.
claims.why: The caller information refers to another module (daedalus.spine.attempt) not present in this chunk; cannot verify.

claims.text: Deliberately delegates rather than being aliased, so a test that monkeypatches _remove_tree_no_follow also intercepts this path.
claims.why: The function body calls _remove_tree_no_follow(root, guarded_ancestors=guarded_ancestors), so monkeypatching the private name affects this wrapper.

claims.text: The ONLY thing reap_branches is allowed to act on. In memory on purpose: the on-disk allocation directory is candidate-writable ... so a record on disk is an attacker-supplied string, not evidence.
claims.why: The trust-model reasoning and the claim that reap_branches only acts on self._allocations is not verifiable in this chunk; reap_branches is not defined here, and the candidate-writable property is not demonstrated.

claims.text: Compared again before every unattended recursive delete -- see _refuse_if_the_primary_checkout_moved.
claims.why: The comparison logic is not in this chunk; the comment refers to a method whose implementation is not shown.

claims.text: A leaf-only check is bypassed by moving the checkout's PARENT instead of the checkout (measured: 40/40 work files destroyed, leaf identity still matching, because the leaf was being read through the junction that had replaced its parent).
claims.why: The measurement and the attack scenario are described but not evidenced in this chunk; the actual ancestor identity checks are not implemented here.

claims.text: It must never refuse a machine's layout -- checkouts legitimately live under redirected profile folders, OneDrive placeholders and developer junctions -- so 'is a reparse point' is not the question asked of an ancestor. 'Is it the same object it was' is.
claims.why: The design rationale is stated, but the actual implementation of ancestor identity comparison is not in this chunk; cannot verify whether it refuses or accepts a given layout.

claims.text: Identity is recorded at CREATION time, because a path string is not an identity -- the manager is the only party that knows what it allocated.
claims.why: The allocation record is written in _record_allocation, which is called before git worktree add (as stated in its docstring and code order: _record_allocation is invoked before the git command in create_worktree, though that is outside this chunk; the code here shows the record includes path and repo).

claims.text: The record lives outside every worktree, so candidate code cannot forge or delete its own, and it is on disk rather than in memory, so a FRESH manager in a NEW process can still clean up a worktree leaked by a crash.
claims.why: The allocation file is placed in worktree_root / ALLOC_DIRNAME, which is outside the worktree (the worktree root is a sibling of the alloc dir, not inside it). The record is written to disk in _write_allocation.

claims.text: Ordering matters for crash-safety: anything that can exist on disk must already have a record, otherwise a crash mid-add leaves a directory that cleanup would (correctly, but uselessly) refuse forever.
claims.why: The ordering claim refers to the call site in create_worktree (not in this chunk) and to cleanup behaviour (also not here). The docstring describes intent, but verification requires the call order.

claims.text: WHAT IT CATCHES: the checkout being moved (or replaced by something wearing its name) between this manager being constructed and a cleanup running.
claims.why: The method body is not in this chunk; only the docstring is shown.

claims.text: HOW IT ANSWERS THAT, AND HOW IT WAS DEFEATED. The question 'is the checkout still the directory I was created for?' is answered by comparing (st_dev, st_ino).
claims.why: The implementation is not in this chunk; the claim is about the method's internals.

claims.text: THREE CHECKS NOW STAND: 1. repo_path MUST NOT BE A REPARSE POINT ... 2. THE LEAF IDENTITY, no-follow ... 3. THE ANCESTOR IDENTITIES, no-follow, calibrated at construction.
claims.why: The docstring describes the method's design, but the actual checks are not implemented in this chunk.

claims.text: Refusing leaks the worktree (and, in the attack, leaves the checkout alive inside it). That is the correct direction: a leak is recoverable by hand, a deleted checkout is not.
claims.why: This is a policy statement; the refusal behaviour is not shown in this chunk.

observations.what: The _remove_tree_no_follow loop re-verifies each directory before removal, but the re-verification only checks reachability and reparse-point status; it does not re-check that the directory is still empty.
remove_tree_no_follow is a public wrapper that delegates to _remove_tree_no_follow; any monkeypatching of the private function will affect the public one, as documented.

GitWorktreeManager.__init__ caches ancestor identities in a list of tuples; the list is not stored as a dict, but the comment says 'the chain above it' is recorded. The comment on _repo_ancestor_identity says it is a list of (parent, identity) pairs, which is consistent.
The allocation record is written before git worktree add, but the code in this chunk does not show the call to _record_allocation; the docstring claims ordering, but the call site is elsewhere.
The _refuse_if_the_primary_checkout_moved docstring is extremely detailed but the method body is not present in this chunk; this is a documentation-only chunk for that method.
